message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | Protium ≈ 99.98 %, Deuterium ≈ 0.02 %, Tritium negligible |
| **Physical State (25 °C, 1 atm)** | State | Gas |
| | Density | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Vapor pressure | 1 atm at 20.28 K |
| **Thermodynamic** | Enthalpy of formation (H₂(g)) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard enthalpy of combustion | –285.83 kJ mol⁻¹ (to H₂O(l)) |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation | –237.13 kJ mol⁻¹ (to H₂O(l)) |
| | Standard entropy | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (H₂(g)) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (in aqueous solution) and a strong base when forming hydride (H⁻). |
| | Redox behavior | Reducing agent (e.g., in the Haber process, water electrolysis). |
| **Bonding & Spectroscopy** | H–H bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Vibrational frequency (H₂) | 4401 cm⁻¹ |
| | Rotational constant (H₂) | 60.853 cm⁻¹ |
| | Dipole moment | 0 (homonuclear diatomic) |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Deuterium (²H) | 2.014 u, heavier, lower zero‑point energy, used in NMR, neutron moderation. |
| | Tritium (³H) | 3.016 u, radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y), used in radiolabeling and fusion research. |
| **Physical Applications** | Fuel cell fuel | H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (electrochemical energy conversion). |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid H₂ + liquid O₂ (high specific impulse). |
| | Metallurgy | Hydrogen embrittlement of steels; used in hydrogen annealing. |
| | Chemical synthesis | Hydrogenation of unsaturated compounds, ammonia synthesis (Haber–Bosch). |
| | Energy storage | Metal hydrides, ammonia borane, liquid organic hydrogen carriers. |
| **Astrophysical & Cosmological** | Most abundant element in the universe | ~75 % by mass. |
| | Role in stars | Fusion of H into He powers stars; proton–proton chain, CNO cycle. |
| | Big Bang nucleosynthesis | First element formed after the Big Bang. |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability range (air) | 4 %–75 % (v/v) |
| | Explosion limits | Lower explosive limit (LEL) 4 %, upper explosive limit (UEL) 75 %. |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but can cause hypoxia by displacing oxygen. |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders (up to 700 bar) or cryogenic tanks (liquid H₂). |
| **Environmental Impact** | Greenhouse gas potential | Negligible (no CO₂ emitted when combusted). |
| | By‑product | Water vapor (clean combustion). |
| | Lifecycle emissions | Depends on production method (electrolysis vs. natural gas reforming). |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest, lightest, and most abundant element** in the universe.
- It exists naturally as a diatomic gas (H₂) under standard conditions.
- Its **isotopes** (deuterium, tritium) have distinct nuclear properties useful in science and industry.
- **Chemically**, hydrogen is highly reactive, forming a vast array of compounds and acting as both an oxidizing and reducing agent.
- **Physically**, it has extremely low density, high volatility, and a very low boiling point, requiring special handling.
- **Technologically**, hydrogen is central to clean‑energy concepts (fuel cells, hydrogen fuel‑cell vehicles, hydrogen‑powered rockets) and industrial processes (ammonia synthesis, petroleum refining).
- **Astrophysically**, hydrogen fusion powers stars and was the first element formed after the Big Bang.

Feel free to ask for deeper details on any specific property or application!
